front: Visual metaphor: an elf waiting for a co-worker to finish can wait in two ways. What are they, the OS counterparts, and the performance cost of each?
back:
• Keep asking "are you done now?" (annoys and delays the worker): a spinlock, repeatedly checking; cost: wasted CPU cycles.
  • Ask to be signaled when done (may be out at lunch, slower to resume): wait for a signal, as with mutexes and condition variables; cost: cache effects when the blocked process comes back to run.

front: Synchronization constructs: why do mutexes and condition variables lack expressive power?
back: You cannot easily express arbitrary synchronization conditions with them. The readers/writer problem needed helper variables to express the access invariants, and helper variables are also needed for priority restrictions, since mutexes and condition variables cannot specify anything about priority.
source: Why Are We Still Talking About Synchronization?

front: Synchronization constructs: what low level support do they require from hardware, and why?
back: Atomic instructions. They are needed to guarantee the correctness of the synchronization construct.
source: Why Are We Still Talking About Synchronization?

front: Spinlocks vs mutexes: what does a thread do when the lock is already held?
back: With a spinlock the thread is not blocked; it spins, running on the CPU and repeatedly checking whether the lock became free. With a mutex the thread relinquishes the CPU and lets another thread run.

front: Spinlock: when does a spinning thread stop burning CPU cycles?
back: When the lock becomes free, or when the thread is preempted for some reason (e.g. its time slice expires or a higher priority thread becomes runnable).

front: Spinlocks: why are they considered a basic primitive?
back: Because of their simplicity, they can be used to implement more complicated synchronization constructs.

front: Semaphore: as a first approximation, what is it like, and what is it initialized with?
back: Like a traffic semaphore (traffic light): it either lets threads go or blocks them, similar to a mutex but more general. It is initialized with an integer value, some positive maximum value.

front: Semaphore: what kind of synchronization requirement does it let you express that a mutex cannot?
back: Count related requirements. For example, allow exactly five producers to produce at the same time by initializing the semaphore with 5.

front: Semaphore: what happens when a thread arrives at a semaphore with a nonzero value vs a zero value?
back: Nonzero: the thread decrements the value and proceeds. Zero: the thread has to wait.

front: Semaphore: what determines how many threads can proceed at a given time?
back: The initialization value of the semaphore. On leaving the critical section a thread signals the semaphore, incrementing its counter.

front: Semaphore: what does a binary semaphore (initialized to 1) behave like?
back: A mutex, allowing only one thread at a time to pass. Posting (incrementing the counter) on a binary semaphore is equivalent to unlocking the mutex.

text: Semaphores were designed by Edsger Dijkstra; the wait and post operations are historically written {{c1::P}} (proberen, to test or try) and {{c2::V}} (verhogen, to increase).

front: POSIX semaphore: name the type and the three operations.
back: Type sem_t; operations create (sem_init), wait, and post/unlock the semaphore.

front: POSIX semaphore: what does the pshared flag indicate?
back: Whether the semaphore is to be shared across processes.

front: Mutex via semaphore quiz: complete sem_init(&sem, ?, ?) so the semaphore behaves like a mutex used by threads within a single process.
back:
sem_init(&sem, 0, 1).
  • pshared = 0: not shared across processes.
  • Initial count = 1: sem_wait decrements and admits exactly one thread at a time into the critical section; sem_post increments, which is identical to freeing the mutex.

front: Reader/writer lock: what access distinction does it make, and what concurrency does each allow?
back: It distinguishes read accesses (do not modify the resource) from write accesses (do modify it). Reads can be shared concurrently; writes require exclusive access.

front: Reader/writer lock: what does the developer specify, versus what the lock handles?
back: The developer only specifies the type of access (read vs write); the lock takes care of access control behind the scenes.

front: Reader/writer locks: what alternate name do some implementations use?
back: Shared/exclusive locks.

front: Linux reader/writer locks: what datatype and operations does the API provide?
back: Datatype rwlock_t; you lock/unlock it for reads and lock/unlock it for writes.

front: Reader/writer locks: name three ways implementations differ in semantics.
back:
• Recursive read locks: one read_unlock releases all of a thread's recursive read_locks vs a separate read_unlock for every read_lock.
  • Priorities: whether a reader that owns the lock gets priority to upgrade to a writer lock ahead of newly arriving write requests.
  • Whether an incoming reader is blocked when a writer is already waiting.

front: Reader/writer lock: where upgrade from read to write is not allowed, what must a reader do?
back: Release its read lock and then contend to re-acquire the lock with write access, competing with any other thread trying to do the same.

front: Reader/writer lock: why might an implementation block an arriving reader even though readers already hold the lock?
back: A waiting writer has higher priority than the arriving reader; an implementation that respects priority may block the reader even though the readers in the critical section would otherwise let it join. The behavior depends on the coupling between lock state, thread priorities, and the scheduling policy.

front: Monitor: what does it specify and what does it do automatically?
back: It specifies a shared resource, the entry procedures to access it, and potential condition variables. On entry/exit it performs all the locking, checking, signaling, and unlocking behind the scenes.

front: Monitor: why is it called a high-level synchronization construct?
back: Because the locking, checking, and signaling are hidden from the programmer; they do not manually invoke lock/unlock or wait/signal.

front: Monitors: historically, which language runtime included them, and how does Java support them?
back: Historically the Mesa runtime (Xerox PARC). In Java every object has an internal lock and synchronized methods are monitor entry points; the one operation still done explicitly is notify.

front: Monitor: besides the high-level construct, what else does the term refer to?
back: The programming style that uses mutexes and condition variables to bracket a critical section with explicit enter-critical-section and exit-critical-section code.

front: Serializers: what do they make easier and what do they hide?
back: They make it easier to define priorities and hide the need for explicit signaling and explicit use of condition variables.

front: Path expressions: how does the programmer specify synchronization behavior?
back: With a regular expression capturing correct behavior (e.g. "Many Reads, Single Write"); the runtime ensures the interleaving of operations satisfies it.

front: Barriers: how do they relate to semaphores?
back: A barrier is like a reverse semaphore: a semaphore allows n threads to proceed before blocking, while a barrier blocks until n threads arrive. Rendezvous points similarly wait for multiple threads to arrive.

front: Wait-free synchronization: what is the optimistic bet, and give a Linux example.
back: It bets there will be no concurrent writes, so reads can proceed concurrently without locking/waiting. Example: read-copy-update (RCU) in the Linux kernel.

front: Synchronization constructs: why is atomically updating a memory location the only foundation they can build on?
back: It is the only way to guarantee that a lock is properly acquired and that state changes are performed in a race-free way.

front: Spinlock quiz 1: spin: if (lock == free) { lock = busy; } else { goto spin; } (free = 0, busy = 1; unlock sets free). Is it correct? Is it efficient?
back:
Neither.
  • Inefficient: while the lock is not free, the goto spin cycle runs repeatedly and wastes CPU.
  • Incorrect: several threads can see the lock free at the same time and all execute lock = busy; one simply overwrites the other, and both enter the critical section.

front: Spinlock quiz 2: while (lock == busy); lock = busy;. Correct? Efficient? What do all purely software spinlocks lead us to conclude?
back: Again neither: it spins continuously while the lock is busy, and once the lock is freed several threads can exit the loop and set it to busy concurrently. No purely software implementation can guarantee the check and set are not interleaved, so we need hardware support to make checking and setting the lock atomic.

front: Spinlock lock: what two steps must happen atomically, and why?
back: Checking the lock value and setting the lock value must happen atomically, so that only one thread at a time can successfully obtain the lock.

front: Why does the naive spinlock (while(lock==busy); lock=busy;) not work?
back: The check and the set take multiple cycles, and during those cycles threads can be interleaved in arbitrary ways.

front: Atomic instructions: name three examples.
back: test_and_set, read_and_increment, compare_and_swap.

front: Atomic instructions: what two guarantees does the hardware make?
back:
• They happen atomically: completely or not at all.
  • Mutual exclusion: cores cannot perform them in parallel; concurrent attempts are queued and performed serially.
In effect, the instruction's operation is the critical section, with the hardware providing all the synchronization for it.

front: Trace while(test_and_set(lock)==busy); for the first thread (busy==1).
back: test_and_set reads the value (initially 0), atomically sets it to 1, and returns 0. Since 0 != busy, the first thread proceeds. Later threads get 1 (busy) back and keep spinning; each of their test_and_set calls sets the lock to 1 again, which is harmless because it was already busy.

front: Atomic instructions: why does software using them need to be ported and optimized?
back: Available atomics vary by hardware (e.g. an increment that does not return the old value, or read_and_decrement instead of read_and_increment), as does their efficiency. Software must use an atomic available on the target platform and use the most efficient one in an efficient way.

front: Shared memory multiprocessor (SMP): what defines it?
back: More than one CPU plus a memory unit accessible to all the CPUs; the memory is shared. Also called a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP).

front: SMP: how do interconnect-based and bus-based configurations differ in concurrent memory references?
back: Interconnect-based (more common today): multiple references can be in flight at once, one per memory module. Bus-based (more common in the past): the shared bus supports only one memory reference at a time, regardless of how many modules are addressed.

front: SMP caches: what do caches do for memory latency, especially in shared memory systems?
back: Caches hide memory latency. The effect is more pronounced in shared memory systems because contention among CPUs for shared memory delays accesses, making cached lookups appear even faster.

front: CPU writes in an SMP: what three options does the lecture describe, and which two are named?
back:
• Do not write to the cache at all: the write goes directly to main memory and any cached copy is invalidated (unnamed in the lecture).
  • Write-through: the write is applied to both the cache and memory.
  • Write-back: the write goes to the cache immediately and to main memory later, e.g. on eviction.

front: Cache coherence: what distinguishes NCC from CC architectures?
back: On non-cache-coherent (NCC) architectures the problem must be handled in software; the hardware will not propagate a write across caches. On cache-coherent (CC) architectures the hardware ensures caches stay coherent after a write.

front: Cache coherence: contrast write-invalidate (WI) and write-update (WU).
back: WI: when one CPU updates X, all other cache entries of X are invalidated; later references on those CPUs miss and go to memory before X is re-cached (memory itself is kept current by write-through or write-back). WU: all cache entries of X are updated, so later accesses hit in the cache and return the new value.

front: Cache coherence: what is the bandwidth advantage of write-invalidate?
back: Lower bandwidth on the interconnect: only X's address is sent (to invalidate), not its value. After one invalidation, further changes to X need no more invalidations, so coherence cost can be amortized over multiple local changes before X is needed elsewhere.

front: Cache coherence: what is the advantage of write-update?
back: X is available immediately on the other CPUs; they avoid a main memory access. Programs that need the new value of X right away on another CPU benefit.

front: Cache coherence: does the software developer choose WI vs WU?
back: No. It is determined by the hardware; the developer has no say.

front: Atomics and caches: where are atomic operations issued, and why?
back: They bypass the caches and go directly to the memory controller/location. This gives a central entry point where references are ordered and synchronized uniquely, eliminating the race conditions possible if atomics updated caches.

front: Why are atomic instructions much more expensive than other instructions on SMP systems?
back: They never leverage the cache, so they always access main memory and contend on it (bus/interconnect contention), and they generate coherence traffic to update or invalidate all cached copies of X regardless of whether X changed (erring on the side of safety).

front: Atomics: the lecture says atomics always bypass the cache. What does Anderson (Section II.A) actually say?
back: That is a teaching simplification. Real atomics cooperate with the cache: under write-back invalidation the atomic obtains the current value from whichever cache holds it dirty while invalidating that copy (avoiding an extra bus transaction to write the data); under distributed-write coherence the needed block is often already cached, so the initial read is skipped and only the final update needs a bus cycle. What is truly unavoidable is the arbitration and coherence traffic: invalidation happens before the instruction executes, even if the instruction does not change the value.

front: Spinlock performance: define latency.
back: The time it takes a thread to acquire a free lock. Ideally immediate, with a single atomic instruction.

front: Spinlock performance: define delay (waiting time).
back: The time required for a thread to stop spinning and acquire a lock that has just been freed. Ideally immediate.

front: Spinlock performance: what does "reduce contention" mean and why does it matter?
back: Reduce contention on the shared bus/interconnect from atomic memory references and the subsequent coherence traffic. Contention delays other CPUs accessing memory and, most importantly, delays the acquisition and release of the spinlock itself.

front: Conflicting metrics quiz: among (1) reduce latency, (2) reduce delay/waiting time, (3) reduce contention, which pairs conflict?
back:
• 1 vs 3: low latency means executing the atomic as soon as possible, which creates additional contention.
  • 2 vs 3: low delay means continuously spinning on the lock to notice the release as soon as possible, which also creates contention.
  • 1 vs 2: not marked; it depends on the algorithm.

front: Test-and-set spinlock: how good is its latency, and why?
back: As good as it gets. It executes only one atomic operation; you cannot do better.

front: Test-and-set spinlock: why is it very portable?
back: test_and_set is a very common atomic that most hardware platforms support, so the same code can run on different hardware platforms.

front: Test-and-set spinlock: how good is its delay?
back: It can perform well. Threads spin directly on the atomic, so the very next test_and_set after the lock becomes free immediately detects it and acquires the lock.

front: Test-and-set spinlock: why does it perform badly on contention?
back: Threads continuously spin on the atomic, so the processor goes to main memory on every instruction, delaying all other CPUs needing memory. Regardless of cache coherence, time is wasted going to memory each test_and_set.

front: Test-and-test-and-set spinlock: what is the key idea, and its other names?
back: Separate the test from the atomic: a CPU tests its cached copy of the lock and only executes the atomic when the cached copy shows the lock became free. Also called spin-on-read or spin-on-cached-value.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Test-and-test-and-set: how does the predicate while(lock==busy OR test_and_set(lock)==busy) work?
back: The first part checks the cached value; while busy the loop stays and the second part is not evaluated. Only when the lock becomes free (first part false) is the atomic actually executed.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Test-and-test-and-set spinlock: how are its latency and delay?
back: Okay, slightly worse than the test-and-set lock, because of the extra step (checking the cached value) before the atomic.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Test-and-test-and-set spinlock: how does contention vary with coherence strategy?
back:
• NCC: no improvement; every reference goes to memory.
  • CC with write-update: improves, but all processors see the lock free at once and rush to lock it.
  • CC with write-invalidate: terrible; each acquire attempt causes memory contention and invalidation traffic.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Test-and-test-and-set: why is contention terrible under write-invalidate specifically?
back: Executing an atomic triggers coherence regardless of whether the value changed. Write-invalidate invalidates the cached copy even if unchanged, forcing a CPU to go to main memory. So any CPU's atomic invalidates all other CPUs, which must then go to memory.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Test-and-test-and-set quiz: with N processors, what is the memory contention on lock release under write-update and under write-invalidate?
back:
• WU: O(N). Everyone sees the release immediately and issues one test_and_set; there are as many memory references as test_and_sets.
  • WI: O(N^2). The release invalidates all caches. Some processors re-read the lock after it is busy again and resume spinning; others re-read it free and issue test_and_set. Only one succeeds, but every one invalidates everybody's caches.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Spin-on-read: whom does Anderson credit for the idea, and what assumption does the paper make explicit?
back: Anderson credits the "spin on read" idea to Segall and Rudolph, not to his own paper; his contribution is analyzing why it still performs poorly, plus the delay and queueing alternatives. The paper also states, as an explicit assumption, the short-circuit evaluation of the loop predicate that the lecture relies on, so test_and_set runs only when the cached read already shows the lock free (Section III.B).
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Spin-on-read: the lecture describes what happens on release. How does Anderson (Section III.B) frame it instead?
back: The weakness is a transient: on release/reacquire there is a "quiesce" period where some processors have a pending read miss and others a doomed test-and-set, and each failing test-and-set re-invalidates every cached copy. For a small critical section this transient dominates, so spin-on-read "has almost as much effect on busy processors as spinning directly on a test-and-set"; for a long critical section the initial slowdown matters less.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Spin-on-read: what did Anderson measure about quiesce time, and what three causes does he list (Sections III.B/III.C)?
back: On the Sequent Symmetry (Fig. 2) the time to quiesce grows linearly with the number of spinning processors. Three distinct causes: (1) the separation between noticing the release and committing to the test-and-set, (2) invalidation on an unchanged value, and (3) the O(P) cost of refilling P caches after one invalidation.
source: Test and Test and Set Spinlock

front: Delay spinlock (delay when lock seen free): what is the rationale and effect on contention?
back: Introduce a delay each time the thread notices the lock is free, to prevent every thread executing the atomic at once. Contention improves significantly; fewer threads see a busy lock as free and attempt a doomed atomic.

front: Delay spinlock (delay when lock seen free): what are its latency and delay like?
back: Latency: okay, similar to before (one reference to cache the lock, one for the atomic). Delay: worse; once the lock is seen free the thread delays for some amount of time, and with no contention that delay is wasted.

front: Alternative delay spinlock (delay after each reference): what is its one benefit and its cost?
back: Benefit: it works on NCC architectures, where every reference goes to main memory, so an artificial delay greatly reduces references while spinning. Cost: it hurts delay much more, since the thread delays on every reference, not just when it detects the lock became free.

front: Static delay: what is the benefit and the drawback?
back: Based on fixed information (e.g. CPU ID). Benefit: simple, and under high load it spreads out atomic references so there is little or no contention. Drawback: unnecessary delay under low contention (e.g. with only CPU 1 and CPU 32 contending, the process on CPU 32 waits about 32 critical-section lengths).

front: Static delay: how is the fixed information (e.g. CPU ID) turned into a delay?
back: It is combined with the length of the critical section: one process is delayed 1x the critical section, another 2x, and so forth.

front: Dynamic delay: how is the delay chosen, and what does it adapt to?
back: Each thread takes a random delay value from a range that increases with the perceived contention in the system, avoiding excessive delays when there is no contention.

front: Dynamic delay: how does the delay range change with contention, and how does dynamic delay behave under high load?
back: Low contention: a small range, so threads back off only a little. High contention: a much larger range, so some back off a little and others for quite a while. Under high load, dynamic delay tends to behave like static delay; theoretically both give the same kind of behavior.

front: Delay: what is a good metric for estimating contention in the system?
back: The number of failed test_and_set operations; more failures imply higher contention.

front: Delay after each lock reference: why can the delay grow misleadingly?
back: It grows not only with contention but also with the length of the critical section: a delayed lock owner or a long critical section makes all spinning threads increase their delays even though contention has not actually risen. The scheme must guard against this case.

front: Delay schemes: the lecture does not say where they come from. What does Anderson (Section IV.A) say?
back: He treats a spin lock as analogous to a CSMA network and borrows network arbitration: statically assigned slots (delay after noticing the release) from BRAM, static mean delays between references from Aloha, and dynamic delay from Ethernet's exponential backoff.

front: Anderson's dynamic delay: how does it adjust a processor's mean delay, and what bounds it?
back: It doubles the mean delay on each "collision" (a failed test-and-set after seeing the lock free), capped at a bound equal to the number of processors, so it degenerates to static slots under heavy contention. Each visit starts at half its previous delay rather than from zero.

front: Delay schemes: why does Anderson call the network-arbitration analogy imperfect?
back: A network collision aborts all parties equally, whereas a test-and-set "collision" still lets one processor win, so the cost depends on how many collide.

front: Queueing lock: what is the core idea for avoiding the thundering herd?
back: Prevent every thread from seeing the lock freed at the same time, which indirectly prevents all threads rushing to acquire it simultaneously.

front: Queueing lock: what data structure does it use and what values do entries hold?
back: An array of flags with up to n elements (n = number of processors). Each element is either has_lock or must_wait. Two pointers mark the current lock holder and the last element on the queue.

front: Queueing lock: how does a new thread get its position, and which atomic is needed?
back: It receives a ticket corresponding to its position, added after the current last element. Because threads may arrive together, queuelast must be incremented atomically, requiring a read_and_increment atomic.

front: Queueing lock: how does a thread wait, and how is the lock handed off on release?
back: The flags element at the thread's ticket index acts as a private lock: while must_wait, it spins; when it becomes has_lock, it may enter the critical section. On release a thread signals the next thread with queue[ticket + 1] = has_lock.

front: Queueing lock: what are its two drawbacks?
back:
• It needs the read_and_increment atomic, which is less common than test_and_set.
  • It needs much more space: n memory locations (one per processor) instead of a single location.

front: Queueing lock implementation: what is it also called, and how is the flags array initialized?
back: The Anderson lock. Initially flags[0] = has_lock and all other elements = must_wait; the lock structure also includes the global variable queuelast.

front: Anderson lock: how does an arriving thread get its index, and where does it spin?
back: It performs the atomic read_and_increment on queuelast, which returns myplace, then spins on flags[myplace mod p] as long as it is must_wait. The very first thread finds flags[0] = has_lock and enters the critical section; threads arriving meanwhile get slots between 0 and p - 1 and spin.

text: Queueing lock: the ticket index is taken {{c1::mod p}} so that queuelast can {{c2::keep increasing}} while the array stays a fixed size.

front: Anderson lock (lecture version): what does the holder do when it is done with the critical section?
back: It resets its own slot flags[myplace mod p] to must_wait (ready for the next thread assigned to that slot), then releases the lock by changing flags[(myplace + 1) mod p] from must_wait to has_lock; the thread spinning there exits its loop.

front: Queueing lock reset: the lecture's narration has the holder reset its slot to must_wait when done with the critical section. Where do Anderson's Table V and the slide do it, and does it matter?
back: Inside the lock routine, immediately after the spin ends (right after acquiring). Either placement works, since no other processor uses that slot until the ticket counter wraps around to it.

front: Queueing lock: why does invalidation on the atomic variable not disturb spinning threads?
back: The atomic involves queuelast, but spinning happens on separate elements of the flags array. Invalidation traffic on cached values of the atomic variable does not concern the spinning, since the atomic and the spinning involve separate variables.

front: Queueing lock: rate its latency, delay, and contention.
back:
• Latency: not efficient; read_and_increment takes more cycles than test_and_set, plus the modular computation of the array index, all before the thread knows whether to spin.
  • Delay: good; each holder directly signals the next element in the queue, and since threads spin on different locations they can spin all the time and notice the change immediately.
  • Contention: much better than all others; the atomic runs once up front, not in the spinning code.

front: Queueing lock: what two conditions are needed to realize its contention gains?
back: A cache coherent architecture (otherwise spinning needs remote memory references), and every array element on a different cache line (otherwise changing one element invalidates the whole line, invalidating caches of processors spinning on other elements).

front: Queueing lock: what key problem of the other spinlocks does it solve, and how?
back: The others let everyone see the lock free at the same time and everyone try to acquire it at the same time. With a separate, essentially private lock per thread in the array, only one thread at a time sees the lock free and only one attempts to acquire it.

front: Queueing lock: lecture presents it as a clear win. What two caveats does Anderson (Section IV.B) add?
back: (1) It worsens the preemption problem: if a spin-waiting process is preempted while in line, every process behind it must wait when it reaches the front before being rescheduled, forcing lock-step behavior for a small, frequently accessed critical section. (2) It makes it harder to wait on multiple locks at once, since a processor can only be in one queue at a time, so it does not adapt to splitting a resource across several locks.

front: Anderson queueing lock: who devised it independently, and why did Anderson's measured version need a backoff lock?
back: Graunke at Sequent. The Symmetry has an atomic increment but no atomic read-and-increment that returns the old value, so Anderson's measurements protected the sequence number with a separate backoff lock.

front: Queueing lock array quiz: with 32 CPUs and flag values has_lock (0) / must_wait (1), is the array 32 bits, 32 bytes, or neither?
back: Neither. Each element must be on a different cache line, so the size depends on the cache line size: e.g. 32 x 64 bytes = 2 KB with 64-byte lines.

front: Spinlock comparison: describe the experiment and platform.
back: Multiple processes each ran a critical section in a loop one million times, with one process per processor. Platform: Sequent Symmetry (20 processors, cache coherent with write-invalidate), which is why the graph caps at 20 processors.

front: Spinlock comparison: what metric is plotted, and how is it defined?
back: Overhead: the measured difference between the observed execution time and the theoretical ideal limit (assuming no delay or contention) for executing the given number of critical sections.

front: Spinlock comparison: which implementations are measured, and which basic lock is left out of the results and why?
back: From spin on read (test_and_test_and_set) to the queueing lock, including the static and dynamic variations of the delay locks. The basic test_and_set lock that spins on the atomic is left out: it would be completely off the charts, with the highest overhead and the worst performance.

front: Spinlock comparison: which lock performs best under high load, and why?
back: The queueing lock. It is the most scalable: as we add more processors and more load, it performs best.

front: Spinlock comparison: which lock performs worst under high load, and what cost accounts for it?
back: test_and_test_and_set. On the write-invalidate platform this strategy forces O(N^2) memory references to maintain cache coherence.

front: Spinlock comparison: how do the delay-based alternatives rank among themselves under load?
back: Static is a little better than dynamic: under high load static delays nicely balance out the atomic instructions, while dynamic randomness causes more collisions. Delaying after every reference is slightly better than delaying after every lock release, because it avoids some additional invalidations on the write-invalidate Sequent Symmetry.

front: Spinlock comparison: under small loads, how do test-and-test-and-set, dynamic delay, and the queueing lock behave?
back: test_and_test_and_set performs well (low latency). Dynamic delay beats static (static naively enforces too-large delays at small loads). The queueing lock performs worst under light load, due to its higher latency: the complex read_and_increment atomic plus extra computation at lock time.

front: Spinlock comparison: what is the closing lesson about choosing a spinlock design?
back: There is no single good answer: design points should be driven by the expected workload (light or high load, architectural features, number of processors, write-invalidate or write-update, and so on).

front: Spinlock graph: lecture blames test-and-test-and-set's cost on O(N^2) references. How does Anderson (Section III.C) describe and bound it?
back: O(N^2) is the lecture's (and quiz's) accounting, not Anderson's notation. He describes the cascade in prose and notes that fixing any one cause alone still leaves "bus activity that grows linearly with the number of processors" (Section III.C). The quadratic total comes from up to P failing test-and-sets, each forcing up to P cache refills.

front: Spinlock graph (Anderson Fig. 3): the basic test-and-set lock is absent from it. Where does the paper show it instead, and what does that figure plot?
back: Only in Fig. 1, which plots elapsed time, not overhead.

front: Spinlock graph (Anderson Fig. 3): what exactly does the paper plot as overhead?
back: Spin-waiting overhead: the elapsed time minus the simulated "ideal" (free spin-waiting) time, which isolates the cost of spinning.

front: Spinlock graph (Anderson): where does the queueing lock's backoff-lock handicap show up?
back: In the separate burst-arrival experiment (Fig. 5), where queueing does not win at high processor counts.

front: Spinlock graph: lecture names the queueing lock the single winner. What is Anderson's headline conclusion?
back: Two winners jointly: backoff and queueing both scale well. Backoff is better with no contention (lower latency); queueing is better when processors are waiting (it parallelizes the lock handoff). Anderson frames the queue's advantage as doing the atomic's work before the lock is released, so throughput can actually rise as the critical section becomes a bottleneck.
